questions: Let's talk about the area where you live. Can you describe your neighbourhood?
What do you like most about living there?
Do you know many of your neighbours?
Is there anything you would like to change about your neighbourhood?
sampleAnswers: It's a fairly quiet residential area on the edge of the city centre. Most of the buildings are five or six-storey blocks of flats, and there's a little square in the middle with a bakery, a pharmacy and a couple of cafés, so it has a bit of a village feel even though it's in a big city.

Probably the convenience. Everything I need day to day is within a ten-minute walk, and there's a metro station just round the corner, so I hardly ever need to use a car. I also like the fact that it's lively during the day but really peaceful at night.

Only a handful, to be honest. I'm on friendly terms with the elderly couple next door, and we chat whenever we bump into each other in the lift, but most people in the building keep themselves to themselves. I think that's quite typical of city life these days.

I'd love there to be more green space. The square is nice, but it's mostly paved, and there isn't a proper park nearby where children can play or people can sit under the trees. Planting a few more trees along the main street would make a real difference, especially in summer.

questions: Now let's talk about handwriting. Do you often write by hand?
Is your handwriting easy to read?
When you were a child, how did you learn to write?
Do you think handwriting will still be important in the future?
sampleAnswers: Not as often as I used to. Most of what I write now is typed, either on my laptop or my phone, but I still write shopping lists by hand, and I always take handwritten notes in lectures because I find it helps me remember things.

It depends on how much of a hurry I'm in. When I take my time it's quite neat, but when I'm taking notes quickly it turns into a bit of a scribble, and sometimes even I can't work out what I've written.

We practised in special exercise books with lines that showed exactly how tall each letter should be. I remember copying the same letters over and over again, which was pretty boring, but the teacher used to give us stickers for neat work, so we were quite motivated.

I think it'll become less important for everyday communication, but I doubt it'll disappear. There's research suggesting that writing by hand helps people learn and remember, and a handwritten card or letter still feels far more personal than a message, so I hope schools keep teaching it.

questions: Let's talk about cooking. Do you enjoy cooking?
What kind of food do you usually cook?
Do you think children should learn to cook at school?
sampleAnswers: I do, especially at the weekend when I'm not in a rush. During the week it's more of a necessity, so I tend to make something quick, but on Saturdays I like trying out a new recipe and taking my time over it. I find it quite relaxing, actually.
Mostly simple home cooking, things like pasta, rice dishes, soups and a lot of vegetables. Every now and then I attempt something more ambitious, like a curry from scratch, with mixed results.

Mainly my dad. He was the one who did most of the cooking at home, and I used to help him chop vegetables and stir things when I was little. When I moved out to go to university, I ended up phoning him for advice almost every evening for the first few months.

Yes, definitely. It's such a basic life skill, and a lot of young people leave home without knowing how to make even a simple meal, so they end up relying on takeaways, which are expensive and often unhealthy. Even a few practical lessons a year would make a big difference.

questions: Now let's talk about the sky. Do you often look at the sky?
Can you see the stars clearly where you live?
Did you learn about stars and planets when you were at school?
Would you like to travel into space one day?
sampleAnswers: More than you might expect. I often glance up when I'm walking home, especially at sunset, because the colours can be amazing. I also have a habit of checking the clouds before I go out to see whether I need an umbrella.

Not really, unfortunately. I live in a big city, and there's so much light pollution that you can only see a few of the brightest stars. The first time I went camping in the mountains I was genuinely shocked by how many stars there were.

Yes, we did a project on the solar system when I was about ten. We each had to make a model of one planet, and I chose Saturn because of its rings, which I made out of cardboard. I've been interested in astronomy, in an amateur way, ever since.

I'd love to see the Earth from space, but I'm not sure I'd have the courage to actually go. The idea of being strapped into a rocket is pretty terrifying. Maybe if space tourism becomes much safer and cheaper, I'd consider a short trip.
